newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to hail decline in deficit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to hail decline in deficit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton planned on Wednesday to hail a dramatic decline in the federal deficit to about $36 billion as proof of the success of his fiscal policies, administration officials said.

Still aglow from signing legislation on Tuesday to balance the budget by 2002 and give Americans a tax cut, Clinton was scheduled to hold his first formal press conference at the White House since March at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on the South Lawn.

"I expect the president will have some encouraging news on our effort to balance the budget and will also speak to his agenda and the important challenges facing us," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.
Senior administration officials, discussing revised projections of the size of the deficit for the current fiscal year, said it would be about $36 billion.
The deficit for fiscal 1996, which ended Sept. 30, stood at $107 billion -- which was substantially below that of the previous year.

Economic forcasters have been predicting a sharp decline in the deficit because of increased revenues. White House Budget Director Franklin Raines on Monday acknowledged that the budget deficit for fiscal 1997 would be below $50 billion.
The federal budget has been in the red every year since 1969.

The White House was hoping the good economic news would take some of the sting out of expected questions from reporters on last year's Democratic fund-raising controversy and ongoing Senate hearings on the matter.
Clinton also planned to use his news conference to promote his upcoming agenda -- including urging Congress to renew his so-called fast-track authority to negotiate international trade agreements.
Under the authority, Congress could either accept or reject any trade accord reached by the administration but would not be allowed to amend portions of it.

Foreign policy also was certain to highlight the news conference, as Clinton works to defuse the latest round of tensions that threaten Middle East peace efforts and moves to deal with famine-stricken North Korea and persuade it to join the United States, South Korea and China in talks on a permanent peace agreement on the divided Korean peninsula.
The White House also announced that National Security Adviser Sandy Berger will meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin in Beijing next week to discuss preparations for an October summit in Washington.
